演奏班蘇裡笛時，笛身通常向右下方斜持，右手食指、中指與無名指按外側指孔，左手同三: To play the bansuri, the flute is usually held slanting down to the right, with the index, middle and ring fingers of the right hand on the outer holes and the same three fingers of the left hand on the rest, supported by the thumbs and little fingers. The blowing hole sits near the lips, and blowing at different speeds changes the pitch and the octave. Six holes give seven basic notes: all closed is the lowest note, then opening the farthest hole, then two, three, four and five, and all open gives the corresponding notes; half-holing gives flattened notes or semitones.

班蘇裡笛傳統琴身取單一空心竹管，竹材經乾燥並以天然油與樹脂處理；吹孔與指孔以熱金: A traditional bansuri is a single hollow bamboo tube, the bamboo dried and treated with natural oils and resins; the blowing and finger holes are burned with a hot metal rod rather than drilled, so the fibres are not damaged. Modern instruments also have bodies of ivory, fibreglass or metal. The sounding body is the air column in the tube; there is no reed. Of the other parts, the source says only that one end is plugged and the body bound with rings, without giving their materials; the decoration or binding thread is silk or nylon.
班蘇裡笛實際可見於印度、斯里蘭卡與尼泊爾的民間歌曲。橫吹式因能較好控制音高、變化: The bansuri is in practice found in folk songs of India, Sri Lanka and Nepal. The transverse type is more used in Indian classical music because pitch, inflection and ornament can be better controlled; the fipple type is mostly folk music, held close to the lips like a whistle. Traditionally it is also often linked with Krishna's rasa lila dance and appears in the religious and dance contexts around it.
班蘇裡笛是源自印度次大陸的古老橫吹竹笛，屬邊棱氣鳴／無簧笛類，Hornboste: The bansuri is an ancient transverse bamboo flute from the Indian subcontinent, among the edge-blown, ductless flutes, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.121.32. It is traditionally made from a single hollow bamboo tube, closed at one end, with a blowing hole near that end and six or seven fingerholes, and no keys; the player opens and closes the holes and changes the pitch with the breath. It is common in folk songs of India, Sri Lanka and Nepal, and the transverse type is also used in Indian classical music.
班蘇裡笛源自印度次大陸，屬橫吹竹笛。早期印度文本以梵語稱之，印尼爪哇與巴里的寺廟: The bansuri comes from the Indian subcontinent and is a transverse bamboo flute. Early Indian texts name it in Sanskrit, and temple carvings in Java and Bali show the same kind of transverse flute. Classical Sanskrit texts of about 200 BCE to 200 CE already discuss the flute. The modern bansuri has changed little since the early Middle Ages; medieval European art shows that it reached Byzantium in the 10th century and from there Europe. After the 15th century, under Islamic rule and West Asian influence, North Indian music commonly used an end-blown manner of playing.
班蘇裡笛靠氣柱共振發聲，吹口在閉端附近，以氣速改變取得不同八度。傳統無鍵，靠按放: The bansuri sounds by resonance of the air column, blown near the closed end, with different octaves obtained by air speed. It traditionally has no keys; the pitch changes by opening and closing the holes and by half-holing. Six holes give seven basic notes, and the range is about two and a half octaves. The size of the bamboo fixes the timbre, longer instruments being lower. The transverse type controls inflection and ornament better, hence its use in Indian classical music; the fipple type is mostly folk music, held like a whistle.
